Current policy · Taxes and migration

Who Leaves Hawaiʻi

Every proposal to ask more of Hawaiʻi’s highest earners meets the warning that they will move away. Eight years of IRS records and the Census Bureau’s survey of who moved show who actually leaves, who arrives and what each group pays.

Hawaiʻi Appleseed · Model run November 25, 2026 · IRS filing years 2015 to 2023; American Community Survey 2020–24

The Warning and the Record

WHEN HAWAIʻI ASKS its highest earners to pay more, the same warning follows: they will leave and take their taxes with them. Hawaiʻi’s income tax already reaches 11 percent on the highest incomes,1 so if high earners move away to escape taxes, it should show here.

Two public records can test the warning. The IRS matches each tax return to the one the same filer sent the year before, so it sees every filer who moves between states and the income they reported.2 The Census Bureau’s American Community Survey asks everyone where they lived a year earlier, in every state, so it sees the people who left Hawaiʻi as well as the people who stayed.3

Both records say the same thing. High earners move to Hawaiʻi faster than they leave, and the people who do leave are young and earn less than the people who stay.

High Earners Arrive Faster Than They Leave

IN EVERY YEAR FROM 2015 TO 2023, more filers with incomes of $200,000 or more moved to Hawaiʻi than moved away: 1,950 more over the eight years. They are also less likely to leave than other filers. In a typical year, 3.7 percent of Hawaiʻi’s $200,000-plus filers moved to another state, against 5.2 percent of all filers.2

The income follows the same pattern. Over the eight years, the $200,000-plus filers who arrived reported $5.6 billion in income in their first year filing from Hawaiʻi. Those who left had reported $2.9 billion in their last.

Across all incomes, more filers leave Hawaiʻi than arrive, about 3,500 a year on net. The ones leaving are not the high earners.

Who Leaves

THE CENSUS SURVEY counts about 32,700 adults a year who lived in Hawaiʻi the year before and now live in another state, and about 27,400 who made the opposite move.3 These counts leave out households with a member on active military duty, whose moves follow orders, and people in dormitories and barracks.

Those who leave are young. Half are 35 or younger, against 51 for adults who stayed. Their median income is $33,500, against $41,800 for both those who stayed and those who arrived.

Most of that gap is age. Compared at the same ages as stayers, those who left averaged $61,500 in income, against $59,000, a difference within the survey’s margin of error. Those who arrived averaged $70,700.

Most of those who leave came from somewhere else: 13 percent were born in Hawaiʻi, against 51 percent of those who stayed. The roughly 4,400 Hawaiʻi-born adults who leave each year are younger still, with a median age of 30 and a median income of $30,600, and 16 percent of them lived below the poverty line. They are not high earners avoiding a tax bill.

The most common destinations are California, Texas, Washington, Nevada and Florida.

The Tax Base That Leaves Is Replaced

TAXED AS IF THEY STILL LIVED HERE, the households that left would owe about $90 million a year in Hawaiʻi income tax under current law. The households that arrived owe about $92 million. The difference, $2 million in the arrivals’ favor, is well inside the survey’s margin of error of about $23 million.

This is not an estimate of revenue lost. The survey asks about income over the past 12 months, so for those who left it is mostly income earned after the move. The table shows the kind of tax base that leaves and arrives, and the two are about the same size.

What These Records Cannot Show

NEITHER RECORD COUNTS MILLIONAIRES WELL. The IRS publishes nothing above $200,000, and the Census survey samples too few millionaires anywhere to count them among those who leave: 17 of its 37,135 Hawaiʻi tax units, and none of the 1,012 who left.

The records also end before Act 24’s brackets take effect in 2027. They test the warning at the tax rates Hawaiʻi already has, which include an 11 percent top rate.

The survey results hold when the groups change. Without households that include a veteran, whose moves may follow military service, the median income of those who left is $30,600. Without 2020’s pandemic-year responses, it is $34,600. Both stay below the median of those who stayed.

What This Means

The record does not support the warning. High earners move to Hawaiʻi faster than they leave, and the people who do leave are young residents with modest incomes, about as well off as stayers their age.

What Hawaiʻi’s highest earners should pay deserves to be decided on its merits. The threat of flight is not one of them.

How These Estimates Are Calculated

TWO SOURCES, each used where it is strongest.4

The IRS figures are the Hawaiʻi rows of the Statistics of Income gross migration files, which compare the address on each return with the same filer’s return the year before. Income is adjusted gross income, in the dollars of each year, and each side’s income is from the year it filed from Hawaiʻi. The files cover filers only, and each filer is in the income class the IRS assigns.

The survey figures come from the American Community Survey’s 2020–24 microdata: every Hawaiʻi resident, and every person in another state who reported living in Hawaiʻi a year earlier, with their households. Each household is split into tax units and taxed under Hawaiʻi’s current income tax and Act 24 with the same model as this site’s other estimates, but on the survey’s own weights, without the adjustments that fit those estimates to Department of Taxation counts, so that people in other states are treated the same way. Incomes are in 2024 dollars.

Download the data

  • irs_flows.csv: filers leaving and arriving, all filers and $200,000 or more, by year (Table 1, Figure 1)
  • irs_by_agi.csv: the IRS’s Hawaiʻi rows, every income class and flow
  • results.csv: every survey estimate with its standard error, including ages, the Hawaiʻi-born and both sensitivity cases (Tables 2 and 3)
  • destinations.csv: where those who left now live
  • manifest.json: run parameters, inputs and code version
